case_title: State of Maharashtra v. Syed Umar Sayed Abbas & Ors.
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.302, 307, 120B r/w s.34; Arms Act ss.25, 27, 29
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (five witnesses); test identification parades; recovery of weapon and ballistic report; post-mortem report
aggravating_circumstances: Multiple gunshot wounds at point-blank range; firing in a crowded public pandal causing commotion
trial_court_outcome: Convicted Accused 1, 3, 4, 9 and 12 under ss.302 and 307 r/w 120-B IPC (1, 3, 4, 12 also under Arms Act s.27; 9 also under s.25); accused 7 and 11 acquitted; sentence not stated
high_court_outcome: Appeals allowed; all accused acquitted of all charges
neutral_facts: On a Saturday afternoon in August 1995, the victim was sitting in a pandal set up for a festival, talking with a person who was the decoration contractor for the pandal. Two unknown persons entered the pandal from a road, were allegedly escorted by three other persons, and opened fire on the victim, firing many bullets into his head, chest and other parts of his body at point blank range. The firing created commotion in the pandal. The contractor tried to run, was hit by a bullet and fell down. The assailants escaped. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead on arrival. The first information report was lodged about an hour and a quarter later by an eyewitness who said he saw the incident from the first floor gallery of a building abutting the pandal. Five eyewitnesses later gave evidence, including the injured contractor. Several witnesses said they identified suspects in test identification parades, which were held roughly a year or more after the incident. The prosecution also relied on recovery of a weapon and a ballistic report. The post-mortem report recorded no injury on the victim's forehead, and the victim had been attacked from behind.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple bullet wounds; the injured eyewitness was hit by one bullet
number_of_offences: 7 charged (IPC ss.302, 307, 120B, 34; Arms Act ss.25, 27, 29); 0 finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: None accepted as clearly establishing identity; the Court upheld the High Court's rejection of the eyewitness and test identification evidence
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PW1, PW4, PW5 and PW6 found unreliable (identification contradictions, delayed parades, doubtful vantage point, commotion, no recollection of appearance); PW7 did not identify any accused at the parade
trial_duration: offence: 12.08.1995; trial judgment: 23.07.2003; High Court: 15.09.2009; Supreme Court: 12.02.2016
legal_representation: For State: Kunal A. Cheema (Addl. Govt. Adv.) with Nishant Ramakantrao Katneshwarkar; for respondents (accused): Mushtaq Ahmad
investigation_status: FIR registered same day at 4:15 PM; investigation completed; charges framed against 13 accused; trial held
procedural_irregularity: Test identification parades delayed by about a year or more and conducted improperly; date discrepancy in PW21's deposition; no joint parade of four accused
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted Accused 1, 3, 4, 9, 12; High Court: acquitted all accused; Supreme Court: State's appeals dismissed, acquittals upheld
prosecution_argument: Trial court judgment was well reasoned; eyewitness and test identification evidence established identity; weapon recovery and ballistic report strengthened the case
defence_argument: High Court rightly gave benefit of doubt; identity not established; test identification parades were delayed, relying on Siddanki Ram Reddy
legal_principle_applied: Where eyewitnesses had little time to see the accused in a crowd or commotion, substantive identification must be corroborated by a prompt test identification parade; delay can be fatal to the prosecution
precedent_relied_upon: Siddanki Ram Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2010) 7 SCC 697
